commenti.body: What are your biggest cinematic blind spots?
For me it’s mostly newer stuff. I’ve only pretty recently dug into film and it’s a whole lot easier to find classic movies than newer ones (Max’s TCM collection is a godsend).
saltburn vs the killing of a sacred deer?

I have never seen a film by bela tarr, edward yang, or Hiroshi Teshigahara , or Cassavetes. Those are some of the most acclaimed directors on rateyourmusic, which has a less populist taste in cinema than Imdb. I also haven't seen any Chantal Ackerman, whose film shot to number one in the sight and sound critic's poll. There are a lot of highly acclaimed films, but if I've seen at least one film by the director it's less of a blind spot for me.

Recommendations for the criterion death race list?

I have The Age of Innocence to see, which is the only TSPDT film on there I haven't seen. Others: Dracula (Francis Ford Coppola), Fallen Angel (these are the two I'm leaning towards), The Glass Key, The Andromeda Strain, The Lodger (1944), The Raven, Murders in the Rue Morgue, Event Horizon, The Mark of Zorro
I have never seen anything by Werner Herzog.

I'm trying to think of the best place to start. Perhaps his single most acclaimed & written-about film, *Aguirre, the Wrath of God*. 

If you do dig into his filmography, you'll discover a very strong thematic connection between his documentaries and his fiction films. In both cases, the decades-long running theme (which you also see in his non-film writing, by the way) is a fascination with obsessed/obsessive people who risk everything (or almost everything) to embark on quests that often only make sense to them. The quest for El Dorado; the transportation of an entire steamboat through the Amazon (note always on water); a human being attempting to truly 'go wild' and live with bears; a community of people who've traveled thousands of miles away from their homes and families and friends to live at an Antarctic research station. 

If that seems like a compelling theme, then Herzog is definitely a filmmaker worth looking into.
*The Age of Innocence* is quite good. As a cinephile (presumably), you'll appreciate its many homages to classic cinema.
Re: Edward Yang, I would highly recommend *Yi Yi,* a film I appreciate more every time I revisit it.
Thanks, I actually really love the wilderness and adventurous quests as themes so I think I know where to look next!
Would highly recommend Fellini. Considered one of the all-time greats for a reason.
I agree. I will do a dive into him at some point

An all-time favorite of mine (that often gets overlooked in the Fellini discography) is *I Vitelloni*. 

Of course, it goes without saying that any cinephile should take the time to watch *La Dolce Vita* and *8 1/2*. 

'Felliniesque' has become a dictionary word for a reason.
Then this might be the perfect next filmography for you to explore!
